title: The Pong machine that jammed with quarters
hook: The first Pong machine broke down because it was stuffed with quarters.
peek: In 1972 Atari put a test Pong machine in a California bar. Within days, the story goes, the bar called to say it had stopped working. The fault was simple: the coin box was overflowing with quarters.
lede: In 1972, the young company Atari built a prototype of Pong, a simple tennis game, and placed it in Andy Capp's Tavern, a bar in Sunnyvale, California. Soon the bar called to say the machine was broken. When engineer Allan Alcorn came to look, he found the cause: so many people had played that the coin box had filled up and jammed.

bullets.text: Atari co-founder Nolan Bushnell gave Pong to Alcorn as a warm-up exercise and, as both later told it, pretended a big electronics firm had ordered it. The result was so much fun that Atari sold it instead.
The prototype's coin box was improvised, and Alcorn's story is that it was a plastic milk container. It filled with quarters until coins backed up and the machine stopped taking them.
Pong's instructions were one short line: avoid missing ball for high score. Two players could work out the game at a glance, which helped it spread through bars far faster than more complex machines.
Pong's simple beeps came from signals already running inside the circuit, because Alcorn had no budget for proper sound. That plain blip became one of the best-known noises in gaming.
